Trigonometric functions. Trigonometric functions—sine, cosine, tangent, and their reciprocals—relate angles in a right triangle to ratios of its sides. They are periodic, oscillating functions fundamental to modeling wave phenomena, circular motion, and oscillatory behavior in physics, engineering, and signal processing.

The six main trig functions are sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, and cotangent. Sine and cosine have period two pi and range from negative one to one. Tangent has period pi and range across all real numbers. Among the most important identities, sine squared theta plus cosine squared theta equals one—this is the Pythagorean identity. The angle sum formulas are sine of alpha plus or minus beta equals sine alpha cosine beta plus or minus cosine alpha sine beta. The double angle formula is cosine of two theta equals cosine squared theta minus sine squared theta. Trigonometric functions are defined on the unit circle. For angle theta, cosine theta is the x-coordinate and sine theta is the y-coordinate of the point at radius one and angle theta. All six trig functions are continuous and differentiable wherever they're defined. The derivative of sine x is cosine x, and the derivative of cosine x is negative sine x. Their applications span from simple harmonic motion in physics to Fourier series used throughout mathematics to AC electrical circuits in engineering, making trigonometric functions indispensable tools across science and engineering.
